votes.rationale: Place value explains how multi-digit magnitudes are represented, making comparison and ordering understandable.
Understanding a fraction as a part of a whole is needed to explain what its numerator and denominator contribute when like fractions are combined.
The concept of area is required to understand and explain what rectangle or square area measures.
Equivalent fractions depend on recognizing that different partitions can represent the same part of a whole.
Equivalent fractions provide the conceptual basis for rewriting fractions with a common denominator before addition or subtraction.
Identifying base and perpendicular height is required to understand the triangle-area formula.
Ratio notation and interpretation are required to understand when two ratios express the same relationship.
Equivalent ratios explain scaling a ratio while preserving its relationship, but dividing a quantity in a ratio can be understood directly from unit parts and totals.
Using a letter for an unknown is required to interpret and explain algebraic expressions containing that letter.
Integer operations provide the conceptual foundation for signs and arithmetic operations when working with negative and non-integer fractions.
Understanding a linear function as y = ax + b is required to explain its graph as a representation of that relationship.
Linear factorisation illustrates reversing the distributive law, which provides a useful bridge to quadratic factorisation but is not necessary.
Prime identification is required to understand why factorisation stops at prime factors.
The specified HCF method explicitly depends on decomposing numbers into prime factors and comparing those factors.
The concept of a linear function is required to understand what a graph of a linear function represents.
Parallelogram area can serve as one possible component formula in composite figures, but composite figures need not contain parallelograms.
Understanding linear functions is required to explain the graph of a linear function as its visual representation.
Quadratic factorisation connects roots and equivalent forms to solving quadratics, but the formula and completing-square methods do not require it.
Forward trigonometric ratios provide an explanatory bridge to their inverse use, but inverse ratios can be understood without first solving for sides.
General trigonometric functions help interpret exact special-angle values, but mastery of all six functions for arbitrary angles is broader than necessary.
Standard derivative notation helps explain and communicate derivatives, but notation alone is not required to understand the power-rule competence.
Derivative notation provides a useful representational bridge to differentiating rational powers, while the differentiation rule can be understood without prior notation mastery.
Basic identities are the direct conceptual basis for transforming and preserving the value of trigonometric expressions during simplification.
The function concept is required to understand exponential and logarithmic expressions as input-output relationships and to interpret their graphs.
Interpreting a derivative as a tangent gradient is required to understand what the listed derivative rules describe.
The standard normal distribution is the reference distribution used to interpret probabilities after standardising a normal variable.
The binomial distribution concept and its modelling conditions are required to explain what its mean and variance describe.
Functions, domains, and ranges are required to understand inverse functions and the reversal of input-output relationships.
Derivative as rate of change is required to understand and explain the meaning of differentiating the listed functions.
The standard normal distribution provides the conceptual reference for calculating probabilities from x₁, μ, and σ.
Direct proof relies on the conditional structure of deriving a conclusion from stated assumptions.
Existential quantifiers express the claim that an object exists, which is the central meaning of a proof of existence.
The polar or exponential representation is required to understand and apply de Moivre’s theorem to powers and roots.
Functions of two variables and their surfaces provide the conceptual setting for changing one variable while holding the other fixed.
Sequence behaviour helps interpret what recurrence solutions generate and how they evolve, but it is not required to solve the stated recurrence form.
Solving first-order linear differential equations gives a concrete example of obtaining solution families, but it is not required for the broader skill of using such families.

enough for none when it provides a defensible explanatory bridge. Do not treat a
merely common teaching order or one optional solution method as necessary.

and source references to define the competence. Parent source bullets are
retained offline as provenance but are omitted from this evidence projection.

as scoped. Do not substitute a narrower hidden subskill for a broader procedural
or conceptual competence. If the stated scope creates a real ambiguity, explain
it in the rationale and still return exactly one class.
Prefer immediate instructional building blocks; if a relation is only a remote
ancestral dependency, explain that limitation rather than assuming a direct link.
Pathways are parallel curricula, not a chronological hierarchy. Earlier source
placement alone is not evidence of necessity. Do not infer an unstated year or
cohort order.
Assumed knowledge can be essential, but does not establish when
it was introduced. Source-uncertain cohort labels do not invalidate otherwise
clear subject content. Classify the skills using all their scope notes.
Do not invent syllabus claims. No web lookup is required. This is only a pilot
and does not imply that omitted pairs are absent from the full prerequisite graph.
